title: The Tollbooth, Then and Now
footnote: Sources: Stripe standard pricing; Amazon 2020 shareholder letter; Marketplace Pulse; FTC v. Amazon (W.D. Wash.)

steps.label: 1. The Alternative Isn't Free
steps.rightText: Own store: card fee ≈ $3.20 + paid traffic (?)
steps.sub: 2.9% + 30¢ to process the card — but the customers still have to be bought on Google, Meta or TikTok.
steps.cue: On your own website, the payment processor
steps.narration: On your own website, the payment processor takes about three dollars on a hundred-dollar sale. Sounds like a bargain... until you realize the customers don't come with it. You have to buy them — one click at a time — on Google, Meta, or TikTok. A different auction... with the same tollbooth logic. And Amazon does deliver something real. Over two hundred million Prime members, fast delivery, and a checkout button people trust without thinking. That's what sellers are paying for.

steps.label: 2. What Changed Is the Price
steps.sub: Amazon's average cut of seller sales (Marketplace Pulse).

evidence.doc: FTC et al. v. Amazon.com, Inc., No. 2:23-cv-01495 (W.D. Wash.)

steps.cue: What's changed is the price. In 2016,
steps.narration: What's changed is the price. In 2016, Amazon's cut was about a third of a seller's revenue. By 2022, it was more than half. And in 2027, a federal judge in Seattle will start deciding whether parts of how Amazon got here broke the law. If the FTC wins, the Buy Box rules could change... and with them, prices across the internet. If Amazon wins, the tollbooth stays.

steps.label: 3. Back to the $100
steps.sub: The fortune belongs to whoever controls the last three seconds before checkout.
steps.cue: So... back to where we started. When
steps.narration: So... back to where we started. When you spend one hundred dollars with a seller on Amazon — who actually gets your money? About ten dollars goes to the business that made the product. About fifty-two goes to the company that owns the shelf. In modern commerce, the company that makes the product rarely gets rich. The fortune belongs to whoever controls the last three seconds before checkout.
